Library reference

Style guide

The components of the library, with a live demo and the markup to copy

This page shows all components of the primer library. A block gives the class names, a line on when to use the component, a live demo and the markup to copy. Use it when you write a chapter, and use it to check that the library has what a new chapter needs.

This page is a reference. The contents of the primer do not list it, it has no previous and next links, and search engines are asked to skip it.

You will need: the chapter starter in primer/lib/starter, and the README of the library in primer/lib for the rules on where a style goes.

How the library is organised

The library is the folder primer/lib. Its styles are eleven files in lib/css, one per family. The build joins them into assets/kit.css. The file lib/kit.js becomes assets/kit.js. A chapter links both. It adds a style file of its own only for figure parts that no other chapter needs.

This page shows all components of the library, in the order of the families below. A block gives the class names, a line on when to use the component, a live demo and the markup to copy. The demos use library classes only. The dashed frame around a demo, the colour swatches and the spacing bars are the only styles that belong to this page. They are in styleguide.css.

FileFamilyShown in
00-tokens.cssThe colour palette in light and darkTokens
05-base.cssReset, page typography, links, headingsTokens, Page shell
10-shell.cssTop bar, hero, intro box, contents, footer, referencesPage shell
20-teaching.cssGuess first, terms, claim, break box, quiz, exercisesTeaching blocks
25-layers.cssThe three layers of a section, try-this lines, the Go deeper fold, the layoutsLayers
30-math-code.cssEquation boxes, typeset maths, code blocks, walk-through panelsMaths and code
40-figure.cssThe card around a figure, controls, layouts, counters, chipsFigure frame
50-tables.cssTable styles and the scroll wrapperTables
60-figdraw.cssParts of an SVG figureFigure drawing vocabulary
70-practice.cssTimer bar, question card, options, resultsPractice set pieces
80-utilities.cssSpacing, text size, colour variables, hidden textUtilities

Four rules keep the library small. A chapter has no style element and no style attribute that a utility class covers. Colours are palette variables, in styles and in scripts. A style that only one chapter's figure needs goes in the chapter's own style file, with the chapter prefix on its class names. When a second chapter needs it, it moves into the library.

The README of the library (primer/lib/README.md) has the full rules: where a style goes, how to add a component, how the build works. When you add a component to the library, add it to this page in the same change. The command python3 primer/lib/build.py --guide-coverage lists the classes this page does not show yet.

Tokens colour, type, spacing

Tokens are the variables that all other styles read. A chapter never writes a colour value. The page also sets one font for text, Spectral, and a monospace stack for code.

Borders and corners

.plain

Borders are 1px lines in the rule colour. Boxes have a 6px corner. Pills and chips have a full round corner. A coloured bar of 3px marks a callout.

  • Border: 1px solid var(--rule), or a 1.5px border on equation boxes.
  • Corner: 6px on boxes and cards, 4px on small tiles, 999px on pills.
  • Callout bar: 3px solid in teal, coral, navy or sand on the left edge.
<ul class="plain">
  <li>Border: <code>1px solid var(--rule)</code>, or a 1.5px border on equation boxes.</li>
  <li>Corner: 6px on boxes and cards, 4px on small tiles, 999px on pills.</li>
  <li>Callout bar: <code>3px solid</code> in teal, coral, navy or sand on the left edge.</li>
</ul>

Page shell

The build writes the shell of a page: the top bar, the title block, the previous and next links, the footer and the scripts. A page.html does not contain them, and the build stops when it does. The demos here are copies, so that a writer can see what the template produces. The intro box, the “you will need” line, the contents list and the references are part of a page's content, and a writer does write them.

Teaching blocks

A teaching section follows one order. It starts with an h2 and a guess-first question, then the new terms and the claim. The figure card follows, with its caption, and then short text on causes and conditions. Equations come next, in two layers. A break box, a debug tip and a code block with output come after them. The section ends with a quick quiz.

Guess first

.ask

One question the reader answers before reading. It starts with a bold “Guess first.” and the figure answers it.

Guess first. A shark twice as long as another: is it twice as heavy, four times, or eight times?

<p class="ask"><b>Guess first.</b> A shark twice as long as another: is it twice as heavy, four times, or eight times?</p>

Terms

.terms

Three to five new terms with a one-line meaning, before the first use. A term list is a dl with one div per term.

length-weight law
weight grows like a power of length
exponent
the power, close to 3 for most fish
residual
the part of a weight the curve does not explain

Claim

.claim

The idea of the section in one sentence, in bold. The figure comes right after it.

A shark twice as long weighs about eight times as much, because weight grows like length cubed.

<p class="claim">A shark twice as long weighs about eight times as much, because weight grows like length cubed.</p>

Caption

.cap

Under a figure. The bold part states the finding. A caption is a statement and has no list of labels.

The curve fits best when the exponent is close to 3. At that value the mean error is 0.3 kg.

<p class="cap"><b>The curve fits best when the exponent is close to 3.</b> At that value the mean error is 0.3 kg.</p>

Break box

.break

A refutation (common belief, why it fails, better account), an analogy (analogy, where it breaks), or a refutation with a detail the reader opens.

Common belief. Twice as long means twice as heavy.

Why it fails. The body also grows taller and wider.

Better account. Weight grows like length cubed.

Analogy. A tree resembles the game of twenty questions.

Where it breaks. A tree may only ask whether a measurement is below a threshold.

Common belief. A bigger model always fits better.

Show the counter-example

A model with a dial per shark fits the training sharks perfectly and misses new ones.

<div class="break">
  <p><b>Common belief.</b> Twice as long means twice as heavy.</p>
  <p><b>Why it fails.</b> The body also grows taller and wider.</p>
  <p><b>Better account.</b> Weight grows like length cubed.</p>
</div>
<div class="break">
  <p><b>Analogy.</b> A tree resembles the game of twenty questions.</p>
  <p><b>Where it breaks.</b> A tree may only ask whether a measurement is below a threshold.</p>
</div>
<div class="break">
  <p><b>Common belief.</b> A bigger model always fits better.</p>

</div>

Debug tip

.debug

A common failure worth spotting, with the first thing to check. Use it where a reader is likely to meet the failure.

Debug tip. If a fit looks wrong, plot the leftovers (the residuals). A pattern in them means the model is missing something.

<div class="debug">
  <p><b>Debug tip.</b> If a fit looks wrong, plot the leftovers (the residuals). A pattern in them means the model is missing something.</p>
</div>

Bridge to my project

.bridge

A short note that ties the chapter to the author's own work. Write it in the first person and take the repeated facts from a snippet.

Bridge to my project. I have built a small robot that ran a vision model on a Raspberry Pi. The same question came up there, and this chapter answers it.

<div class="bridge">
  <p><b>Bridge to my project.</b> {{snippet:robot-fact}} The same question came up there, and this chapter answers it.</p>
</div>

Used in, and In practice

.used

A used line closes a toolkit section and points to the chapters that use the idea. A paragraph that starts with a bold “In practice” gives the working rule.

Used in: the line has two dials and is the model of A2. A neuron in B1 is the same idea with a bend added.

In practice, choose the depth with cross-validation on the training sharks (A4), and keep the simplest tree whose score is close to the best.

<p class="used"><b>Used in:</b> the line has two dials and is the model of <a href="../a2-linear-regression/#line">A2</a>. A neuron in <a href="../b1-one-neuron/#neuron">B1</a> is the same idea with a bend added.</p>
<p><b>In practice</b>, choose the depth with cross-validation on the training sharks (<a href="../a4-grading-models/#cv">A4</a>), and keep the simplest tree whose score is close to the best.</p>

Try this

Layers three layers, three layouts

A teaching section can be written in three layers. Layer 1, the idea, is what a reader needs to stop with. Layer 2, how it works, gives the example, the equation, where the idea breaks and two check questions. Layer 3, go deeper, is one closed fold. The figures are the ones of the section and do not change.

  1. A layered section
  2. Layouts and the v parameter

A layered section

.layer .layer-idea .layer-how .layer-h .try .deeper .deeper-what .deeper-time .deeper-body

One section in three layers. The idea is a question, up to three terms, the key sentence, the figure with one to three try-this lines in its card, and the finding. How it works has a heading, two to five short blocks and a quick quiz of two questions. Go deeper is one closed fold with the rest. The demo is a working section: add ?v=beside or ?v=steps to the address of this page to see it in another layout.

Weight from length

Guess first. A shark twice as long as another: is it twice as heavy, four times, or eight times?

exponent
the power in the rule, close to 3 for most fish
length cubed
length times length times length

A shark twice as long weighs about eight times as much, because weight grows like length cubed.

  1. Read the first two bars. The bar of 80 cm is eight times the bar of 40 cm.
  2. Read the last bar. A shark of 160 cm weighs eight times as much as one of 80 cm.
40 cm
0.26
80 cm
2.05
160 cm
16.4

Doubling the length multiplies the weight by 8. Weights are in kg and made up.

How it works

Step by step. Doubling the length doubles three sides of a box. The weight is multiplied by 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.

8weight, times=2length×2width×2height

Common belief. Twice as long means twice as heavy.

Why it fails. The body also grows taller and wider.

Better account. Weight grows like length cubed.

Quick quiz

A shark three times as long weighs about how many times as much?

About 27 times, since three cubed is 27.

Why can a line not fit weight against length well?

Weight grows faster than length, so the points bend upwards.

Go deeper symbols, Python about 1 min

Symbols

\[ W = a\,L^{3} \]

  • \(W\) is the weight in kg and \(L\) is the length in cm.
  • \(a\) is the dial that data sets. Its value here is 0.000004.

In Python

import numpy as np

lengths = np.array([40, 80, 160])      # cm
weights = 0.000004 * lengths ** 3      # kg
print(weights)
[0.256 2.048 16.384]

Common mistakes

Debug tip. The dial has units. If all weights are a thousand times too large, look for grams mixed with kilograms.

Layouts and the v parameter

?v=layers ?v=beside ?v=steps

The same words show in three layouts. A small script in the head reads ?v= and sets data-layout on the html element before the page paints. Without the parameter the layout is layers. Links to other chapters keep the parameter. Without JavaScript the page shows all of it, in the order of the layers.

ParameterLayoutWhat the reader sees
layersLayers, the defaultThe layers one under the other. Go deeper is a closed fold.
besideBesideFrom 1180 px wide, the text on the left and the figure of layer 1 pinned on the right while the section scrolls. The try-this list leaves the pinned card and goes to the left column, after the key idea. A card that is taller than the window height minus 40 px (counted without its list), wider than its column, inside a box that scrolls, or marked data-nopin stays in the text and spans both columns, with its list back in the card. Below 1180 px it equals layers.
stepsStepsLayer 1 stays open. Layer 2 shows its heading, then one step at a time. A button reveals the next step, and Show all steps reveals them all. Go deeper appears after the last step.

Classes the script adds

.js .kit-ready .layer-shown .layer-all .layer-next .layer-btn .layer-count .layer-nopin

A page never writes these. .js is on the html element when the head script ran. .kit-ready comes when kit.js has finished its start. If it has not come four seconds after load, the head script removes .js and returns the layout to layers, so layer 2 and the fold show. .layer-shown marks a step, or the fold, that the Steps layout has revealed. .layer-all is the Show all steps button. .layer-next is the bar under the visible steps, with the Next button .layer-btn and the count .layer-count. .layer-nopin marks a card that Beside has taken out of the right column. A link to an element inside the fold opens the fold, and a script can call Kit.openFold(el). The check python3 primer/lib/check_layers.py tests the markup rules, and node primer/lib/check_layout.mjs checks the layouts in a browser.

Typeset maths with symbol notes

.math .math-notes

The general formula in KaTeX, then a list that names all symbols in plain words. Write a displayed formula between \[ and \], and an inline formula between \( and \).

\[ W = a\,L^{b} \qquad\qquad \hat y = w x + b \]

  • \(W\) is the weight and \(L\) the length of a shark.
  • \(a\) is a constant that sets the scale, and \(b\) is the exponent: about 3, since a shark grows in length, height and width together.
  • \(\hat y\) is the model's guess for the weight, from the dials \(w\) and \(b\).
<p class="math">\[ W = a\,L^{b} \qquad\qquad \hat y = w x + b \]</p>
<ul class="math-notes">
  <li><b>\(W\)</b> is the weight and <b>\(L\)</b> the length of a shark.</li>
  <li><b>\(a\)</b> is a constant that sets the scale, and <b>\(b\)</b> is the exponent: about 3, since a shark grows in length, height and width together.</li>
  <li><b>\(\hat y\)</b> is the model's guess for the weight, from the dials <b>\(w\)</b> and <b>\(b\)</b>.</li>
</ul>

Runnable code

.code .out

Add data-run to a code block and the reader gets a run button. The first run loads Python into the page, about 10 MB. Keep runnable blocks short and NumPy only. Press run.

import numpy as np

L = np.array([40, 60, 80, 100])        # length, cm
W = 0.004 * L ** 3                      # weight, g
b, log_a = np.polyfit(np.log(L), np.log(W), 1)
print(f"b = {b:.2f}, a = {np.exp(log_a):.4f}")
b = 3.00, a = 0.0040

      <span class="ln dim">print("done")</span>
    </div>
  </div>
  <div>

      <div class="vb gone"><small>L</small><b>80</b></div>
      <div class="vb err"><small>totl</small><b>NameError</b></div>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

Figure frame

The card contains a figure, its controls and its numbers. Controls are built with the Kit helpers, so that they look the same on all pages. Plots are drawn with Kit.plot, which reads the palette. Pages never draw their own axes colours.

  1. Card with Kit controls and a plot
  2. Plot with the palette
  3. Bar items
  4. Check boxes
  5. Readout and status
  6. Two-column layouts
  7. Counter tiles
  8. Token chips
  9. Value bars, ranked rows and segments
  10. Figure helpers
  11. Pixel canvas
  12. Older figure parts

Card with Kit controls and a plot

.card .controls .bar .label .check .plot .short .readout .status Kit.slider Kit.select Kit.chips Kit.button Kit.plot .group .btn

A card with a slider, a menu, chips, a button and a check box, a plot, a readout and a status line. Kit.slider, Kit.select, Kit.chips and Kit.button write the controls. Move the exponent, or press Play.

Show
Mean error: 0 kgExponent: 3.0

<div class="card" id="gd-card">
  <div class="controls" id="gd-controls"></div>
  <div class="bar" id="gd-bar"><span class="label">Show</span></div>
  <div class="bar"><label class="check"><input type="checkbox" id="gd-resid"> mark the errors</label></div>
  <div class="plot short" id="gd-plot" role="img" aria-label="Weight against length for made-up sharks, with a curve whose exponent you can change"></div>
  <div class="readout"><span>Mean error: <b id="gd-err">0</b> kg</span><span>Exponent: <b id="gd-exp">3.0</b></span></div>
  <p class="status" id="gd-status" aria-live="polite"></p>
</div>
var show = 2;                                   // 0 points, 1 curve, 2 both
var b = Kit.slider(Kit.$("gd-controls"), {label: "Exponent b", min: 1, max: 4, step: 0.1, value: 3}, draw);
Kit.select(Kit.$("gd-controls"), "Curve colour", [{value: "coral", label: "coral"}, {value: "teal", label: "teal"}], "coral", draw);
Kit.chips(Kit.$("gd-bar"), ["Points", "Curve", "Both"], 2, function (i) { show = i; draw(); });
Kit.button(Kit.$("gd-bar"), "Play", function () {
  Kit.animate(1600, function (p) { b.set(1 + 3 * Kit.ease(p)); draw(); });
});
function draw() {
  Kit.plot("gd-plot", function (P) { return [/* points in P.navy, curve in P.coral */]; },
           {xaxis: {title: {text: "length, cm"}}, yaxis: {title: {text: "weight, kg"}}});
}

Plot with the palette

.card .plot .tall

Kit.plot takes traces and a layout, or functions of the palette P, so the colours follow the theme. Five series colours come in this order. The plot area has three heights: short, default and tall.

<div class="card">
  <div class="plot tall" id="gd-plot2" role="img" aria-label="Five curves drawn in the five series colours: navy, coral, teal, sand and grey"></div>
</div>
Kit.plot("gd-plot2", function (P) {
  return P.series.map(function (c, i) {
    return {x: xs, y: ys(i), mode: "lines", name: names[i], line: {color: c, width: 3}};
  });
}, {showlegend: true, xaxis: {title: {text: "x"}}, yaxis: {title: {text: "y"}}});

Figure drawing vocabulary

The classes in 60-figdraw.css style the parts of an SVG figure: axes, grid, labels, series and markers. They apply inside an svg with the fg class, and the generated figures of the practice sets use them. A chapter figure may use them too. Put the svg in a pfig box, which limits its width and centres it. Colours follow the palette, so the figure follows the theme.

Practice set pieces

The six practice sets share a timer bar, a question card, options and a results block. All of it applies inside pset, the class that the template puts on main for a practice set. The demos below are inside a pset container. Two classes from the figure frame, btn and btn-main, are used here too.

  1. Timer bar
  2. Question card and options
  3. Number and code questions
  4. Figures inside a question
  5. Results

Timer bar

.pset .pbar .pb-time .btn .pb-prog .wide .pb-jump .mt-12 .over

The bar sticks to the top of the screen while the reader works. The pb-time class turns coral when the time is over.

42:10 7 of 25 answered Score
61:05 25 of 25 answered Score 
<div class="pset">
  <div class="pbar" role="group" aria-label="Timer and progress, demo">
    <span class="pb-time" role="timer">42:10</span>
    <button type="button" class="btn">Pause timer</button>
    <span class="pb-prog"><b>7</b> of 25<span class="wide"> answered</span></span>
    <a class="pb-jump" href="#practice">Score</a>
  </div>
  <div class="pbar mt-12" role="group" aria-label="Timer, over time">
    <span class="pb-time over">61:05</span>
    <span class="pb-prog"><b>25</b> of 25<span class="wide"> answered</span></span>
    <a class="pb-jump" href="#practice">Score</a>
  </div>
</div>

Question card and options

.pset .pq .pq-h .pq-st .pq-tag .pq-t .opts .sr .opt .on .revise .right .mt-14 .missed

A question is an article with a heading, a text and options. Options are radio buttons in a fieldset. The on class marks the picked option. After scoring, the card gets right or missed.

Question 1Models and baselines

A model scores 52% on 58 dive records. A model that always says bamboo scores 55%. Which statement is correct?

Choose one answer

Revise A1.

Question 2RightDecision trees

A split sends 21 sharks to one side and all of them are other sharks. What is the Gini score of that side?

Choose one answer

Question 3MissedBoosting

Boosting adds trees one after another. What does a new tree fit?

Choose one answer

Revise A6.

<div class="pset">
  <article class="pq" id="gd-q1">
    <h3 class="pq-h"><span>Question 1<span class="pq-st" hidden></span></span><span class="pq-tag">Models and baselines</span></h3>
    <p class="pq-t">A model scores 52% on 58 dive records. A model that always says bamboo scores 55%. Which statement is correct?</p>
    <fieldset class="opts"><legend class="sr">Choose one answer</legend>
      <label class="opt"><input type="radio" name="gd-q1" value="0"><b>A</b><span>The model beats the always-bamboo model, because 52% is a large number.</span></label>
      <label class="opt on"><input type="radio" name="gd-q1" value="1" checked><b>B</b><span>The model does worse than the always-bamboo model on the dive records.</span></label>
      <label class="opt"><input type="radio" name="gd-q1" value="2"><b>C</b><span>The two models cannot be compared on 58 records.</span></label>
    </fieldset>
    <p class="revise" hidden>Revise <a href="../a1-what-is-a-model/">A1</a>.</p>
  </article>
  <article class="pq right mt-14" id="gd-q2">
    <h3 class="pq-h"><span>Question 2<span class="pq-st">Right</span></span><span class="pq-tag">Decision trees</span></h3>
    <p class="pq-t">A split sends 21 sharks to one side and all of them are other sharks. What is the Gini score of that side?</p>
    <fieldset class="opts" disabled><legend class="sr">Choose one answer</legend>
      <label class="opt on"><input type="radio" name="gd-q2" checked disabled><b>A</b><span>0</span></label>
      <label class="opt"><input type="radio" name="gd-q2" disabled><b>B</b><span>0.5</span></label>
    </fieldset>
  </article>
  <article class="pq missed mt-14" id="gd-q3">
    <h3 class="pq-h"><span>Question 3<span class="pq-st">Missed</span></span><span class="pq-tag">Boosting</span></h3>
    <p class="pq-t">Boosting adds trees one after another. What does a new tree fit?</p>
    <fieldset class="opts" disabled><legend class="sr">Choose one answer</legend>
      <label class="opt on"><input type="radio" name="gd-q3" checked disabled><b>A</b><span>The original weights</span></label>
      <label class="opt"><input type="radio" name="gd-q3" disabled><b>B</b><span>The errors of the trees so far</span></label>
    </fieldset>
    <p class="revise">Revise <a href="../a6-boosting/">A6</a>.</p>
  </article>
</div>

Number and code questions

.pset .pq .pq-h .pq-st .pq-tag .pq-t .tight .pq-code .pq-num .u .mt-14 .stm .wrap

A numeric answer has a text input with a unit. A statement list gives claims to judge. A code question shows the program in pq-code, which wraps with the wrap class.

Question 4Toolkit

What does this program print?

dives = [4, 1, 3]
same = dives
same.append(dives[0] + dives[2])
print(len(dives))

Question 5Grading

Which statements are true?

  • A test set is used to choose the dials.
  • A held-out set is not seen during training.
score = (predictions == labels).mean()   # a long line wraps inside the card when the wrap class is set
<div class="pset">
  <article class="pq" id="gd-q4">
    <h3 class="pq-h"><span>Question 4<span class="pq-st" hidden></span></span><span class="pq-tag">Toolkit</span></h3>
    <p class="pq-t tight">What does this program print?</p>
    <pre class="pq-code">dives = [4, 1, 3]
same = dives
same.append(dives[0] + dives[2])
print(len(dives))</pre>
    <label class="pq-num"><span>Your answer</span><input type="text" inputmode="decimal" autocomplete="off" aria-label="Answer to question 4"><span class="u">numbers</span></label>
  </article>
  <article class="pq mt-14" id="gd-q5">
    <h3 class="pq-h"><span>Question 5<span class="pq-st" hidden></span></span><span class="pq-tag">Grading</span></h3>
    <p class="pq-t tight">Which statements are true?</p>
    <ul class="stm"><li>A test set is used to choose the dials.</li><li>A held-out set is not seen during training.</li></ul>
    <pre class="pq-code wrap">score = (predictions == labels).mean()   # a long line wraps inside the card when the wrap class is set</pre>
  </article>
</div>

Utilities

Small single-purpose classes in 80-utilities.css. They replace inline style attributes, so they win over component rules. Use a utility before you write a style attribute.

  1. Spacing
  2. Text size, width and labels
  3. Colour variables

Spacing

.counts .mt-6 .mt-8 .mt-10 .mt-12 .three .mt-14 .m-b4 .m-b8

Margin above in pixels (mt-6 to mt-14), and the tight paragraph (m-b4, m-b8: no margin above, 4px or 8px below). The tiles below start lower as the class grows.

6mt-6
8mt-8
10mt-10
12mt-12
14mt-14

m-b4

m-b8 below it

Two tight paragraphs

in one tile

<div class="counts">
  <div class="mt-6"><b>6</b><span>mt-6</span></div>
  <div class="mt-8"><b>8</b><span>mt-8</span></div>
  <div class="mt-10"><b>10</b><span>mt-10</span></div>
  <div class="mt-12"><b>12</b><span>mt-12</span></div>
</div>
<div class="counts three">
  <div class="mt-14"><b>14</b><span>mt-14</span></div>
  <div><p class="m-b4"><b>m-b4</b></p><p class="m-b8">m-b8 below it</p></div>
  <div><p class="m-b8">Two tight paragraphs</p><p class="m-b4">in one tile</p></div>
</div>

Text size, width and labels

.fg .fs-13 .tbl .mw-36 .mt-12 .bar .label-block .hide-s .btn .sr

The class fs-13 sets 13px on SVG text, where a class rule would lose against the figure rule. The class mw-36 caps a table at 36em. The class label-block puts a label on its own line above a control. The class hide-s hides a part below 600px. The class sr hides text from the eye and keeps it for screen readers.

Colour variables

.legend-line .tint-navy .tint-coral .tint-teal .tint-sand .tint-ink

The tint classes set the colour variable of a legend swatch or a coloured box. They replace a style attribute that set the variable.
